title: Where are they?
text: The recall of the ex-regular reserve is under way. Only 34,755 of the estimated 95,000 people said to hold a Strategic Reserve liability appear on any current record. The Department believes it holds a usable address for perhaps half of the remainder. Nobody can say how many of those are alive, in the country, or under the recall age.

choices.label: Spend a month tracing
choices.summary: Costs political capital and a month of staff time; some of the untracked pool is found and reports at low effectiveness.

choices.label: Move on
choices.summary: The untracked remain untracked and the figure stays in the press.

source.name: MoD Service Personnel Statistics, 1 July 2026, Table 8a; Forces News, 15 January 2026

title: The ninety-day amendment
text: A backbench amendment to the Armed Forces Bill would cut the Army Reserve's standard notice from 180 days to 90. The Treasury opposes it: employers would claim sooner and for longer. The Whips' Office reports that the numbers are close and that your view will decide it.

choices.label: Back the amendment
choices.summary: Costs political capital with the Treasury; the reservists already called out arrive three months sooner.

choices.label: Let it fall
choices.summary: No cost now; the reservists arrive on the original timetable.

source.name: Armed Forces Bill 2026, amendment papers (Select Committee, 14 April 2026; Public Bill Committee, 16 April 2026)

title: The instructors' revolt
text: Three commanding officers have written, through the chain of command and then around it. Each has lost about a third of his section commanders to the training estate and expects to lose more. The letter uses the word hollow. It has been shown to the Chief of the General Staff. He did not disagree with it.

choices.label: Accept the cost
choices.summary: The field army stays hollowed out; the leadership factor over every conscript cohort falls.

choices.label: Return a tranche of instructors
choices.summary: One capacity expansion is stood down and its junior leaders go back to their units.

title: A death on the Phase One run
text: A conscript with an undiagnosed cardiac condition collapsed and died during a Phase One fitness test on Tuesday. He had been passed fit under the wartime standard. The coroner has opened an inquest; the family have a solicitor and a newspaper. The Surgeon General's office asks, in writing, whether the standard is to remain.

choices.label: Restore the peacetime standard
choices.summary: The eligible pool shrinks and training attrition falls; the inquest loses its headline.

choices.label: Hold the line
choices.summary: The standard stays; the cost is political and it is paid now.

title: The first objector
text: The first conscientious-objection case under the Act has reached the High Court. The applicant is articulate, photogenic and a nurse. Counsel advise that the exemption schedule is defensible but that the judge may not be. The hearing is next week.

choices.label: Concede a broad exemption
choices.summary: The eligible pool shrinks by a tenth; the Government is seen to be reasonable.

choices.label: Contest the case
choices.summary: Costs political capital to fight; an even chance of winning modestly or losing badly.

title: A letter from the Chancellor
text: The Chancellor has written to the Prime Minister, copying you as a courtesy. The letter notes that the mobilisation is now the largest unfunded commitment on the books and asks what is to be stopped to pay for it. It runs to two pages. The second page is a list.

choices.label: Stand down a capacity tranche
choices.summary: One training expansion is cancelled and the letter is answered.

choices.label: Fight for the money
choices.summary: The Prime Minister backs you, at a price in political capital.

title: The ally asks
text: The ally's defence minister has telephoned. He asks, politely and for the second time, whether the division will be on the ground on the date agreed. His chief of staff is on the line taking notes. A holding answer is not available.

choices.label: Tell him where you are
choices.summary: The figures are shared as they stand; he is reassured, up to a point.

choices.label: Promise it
choices.summary: A boost now; a heavy cost at the reckoning if the target is missed.

title: The ally asks, again
text: The ally's defence minister has telephoned. He has seen the figures in the press and asks whether they are right. His chief of staff is on the line taking notes. A holding answer is not available, and the figures are right.

choices.label: Tell him the truth
choices.summary: He is not reassured; some political cost now, none later.

choices.label: Promise it anyway
choices.summary: A boost now; a heavy cost at the reckoning if the target is missed.

title: A slip on body armour
text: The body-armour supplier reports a two-month slip on the emergency order. The plates are fine; the ceramic supplier's ceramic supplier is not. The contract has penalty clauses. The penalty is money, and money does not make ceramic.

choices.label: Accept the slip
choices.summary: Equipment arrives two months later than planned; trained conscripts wait unequipped.

choices.label: Source abroad
choices.summary: Costs money and a little political capital; the original date holds.

title: A bounce in the polls
text: The pollsters report a rise in the share of the public who say they would serve if asked. Number Ten attributes it to your address. The pollsters attribute it to the weather and a football result. It will not last.

choices.label: Noted
choices.summary: Willingness to serve rises for a few months.

title: The wards close
text: Three NHS trusts report ward closures attributable to mobilised reservists: theatre nurses, anaesthetists, a paediatric consultant. The Health Secretary has raised it in Cabinet. The reservists in question are exactly the ones the field hospital needs.

choices.label: Exempt clinical staff
choices.summary: Around two thousand reservists are released back to the NHS.

choices.label: Hold them
choices.summary: The wards stay closed and the political cost is paid.

title: The Strategic Reserve on paper
text: In January the maximum recall age for the Strategic Reserve was raised to 65, on the basis that an estimated 95,000 former personnel hold a liability to serve. The Department can write to 34,755 of them. Efforts to improve the contact information are, in the words of the impact assessment, under way.

choices.label: Write to every last address
choices.summary: A small political cost now; a few more ex-regulars report when recalled.

choices.label: Wait for the records
choices.summary: Nothing changes; the records do not improve on their own.

source.name: MoD press release, 15 January 2026; Forces News, 15 January 2026; MoD SPS 1 July 2026, Table 8a

title: The £110 cap
text: Employers of mobilised reservists may claim financial assistance for replacement costs, capped at £110 a day under regulations made two decades ago. Small-business representatives say the cap has not moved since and that a locum costs a multiple of it. Several employers have written to say they will contest the call-out papers.

choices.label: Raise the cap
choices.summary: Costs money for the length of the mobilisation; the employers go quiet.

choices.label: Hold the cap
choices.summary: A handful of appeals succeed, a few hundred reservists go home, and some political capital is spent.

source.name: Reserve Forces (Call-out and Recall) (Financial Assistance) Regulations 2005, SI 2005/859, regulation 6(3)

title: Idle in barracks
text: A newspaper has photographs from inside a barracks where several thousand conscripts have been waiting for a training place for weeks. Card games, a broken boiler, a sergeant who has not been home since the call-out. The caption says the Army does not know what to do with them. Nobody in the Department can say otherwise.

choices.label: Send the surplus home
choices.summary: A fifth of the holding pool is released on deferred call-up; a little political capital is spent.

choices.label: Keep them
choices.summary: They stay, they are paid, they produce nothing, and the story runs for a month.

title: Trained, unequipped
text: The first conscript cohorts have completed Phase Two. They are parading in training-issue clothing with no body armour, no helmets to scale and rifles on loan from the schools. No emergency equipment order has been placed. Until one is, they are not soldiers you can send anywhere.

choices.label: Take the hit
choices.summary: The political cost of the photographs, and nothing else changes.

choices.label: Blame the supply chain
choices.summary: An even chance it works; if it does not, the cost doubles.

title: Corporals on rotation
text: The junior NCOs running Phase One have been on a six-day week since the call-out and are sleeping in the accommodation blocks. Two have been medically downgraded this month, and one has resigned in a manner involving a fire extinguisher. The commandant asks for either more people or fewer recruits.

choices.label: Rest the instructors
choices.summary: Throughput dips for two months while the rota is rebuilt.

choices.label: Press on
choices.summary: The rota holds; more junior leaders are stripped from the field army and a little political capital is spent.

title: A shorter course, the same instructors
text: Phase One was 14 weeks before the crisis. Compressing it has not reduced the number of section commanders needed to run it. It has only reduced the time each of them has to make a soldier. The training schools report that they can fill the extra intake places or staff them, but not both.

choices.label: Accept the shortfall
choices.summary: Throughput falls for a few months while the schools staff up.

choices.label: Strip the field army
choices.summary: More junior leaders are pulled into the schools; the leadership factor over the conscript force drops.

source.name: House of Lords written question HL1629, answered 26 February 2020

title: The Public Accounts Committee
text: The Committee has summoned the Department. Its brief notes that the last published cost of training a Phase One recruit was £47,800. It asks what the emergency programme is spending per head, and why nobody can say. The chair has a reputation. The hearing is televised.

choices.label: Send the Permanent Secretary
choices.summary: The Accounting Officer takes the hearing; a modest political cost.

choices.label: Appear in person
choices.summary: A gamble: a good hearing earns credit, a bad one costs more.

source.name: Written answer (Luke Pollard MP to James Cartlidge MP), FY2023-24 Phase 1 cost at ATC Pirbright, as reported by UK Defence Journal, 22 October 2024

title: The employers' letter
text: The employers' organisations have written jointly, using the Treasury's own figures: each person removed from the workforce is worth £51,100 a year in wages alone and £88,800 in output. They note that the Government is removing the youngest and the healthiest, and ask which industries are to be protected.

choices.label: Widen the exemptions schedule
choices.summary: The eligible pool shrinks by a tenth; the employers are placated.

choices.label: Refuse
choices.summary: The letter is published; some political cost.

source.name: ONS: compensation of employees 2025 (DTWM) per employee (MGRN); GDP 2025 (YBHA) per person in employment (MGRZ)

title: Judicial review
text: A coalition of charities has been granted permission to seek judicial review of the exemptions schedule. Their case is that a minimal schedule is irrational and that the consultation lasted a fortnight. Counsel say the Department has a case. Counsel are paid to say that.

choices.label: Defend it
choices.summary: An even chance: a win earns a little credit; a loss costs more and the court widens the schedule for you.

choices.label: Settle
choices.summary: The schedule is widened to the broad regime now; a small political cost.

title: The devolved administrations
text: The First Ministers have issued a joint statement that the Act was passed without consent and that their governments will not assist with registration. The statement has no legal force. It has a great deal of political force. The territorial departments ask for a line.

choices.label: Negotiate
choices.summary: Some local flexibility is conceded and a small share of the pool is lost.

choices.label: Overrule
choices.summary: Political cost, and willingness to serve dips for a time.

title: The liaison team
text: A NATO liaison team spent three days with the new formations. Their report is polite. It counts the bodies, then counts the sergeants, and notes the ratio without further comment. It has been copied to the ally.

title: This note has leaked
text: Last month's briefing note is on the front page. The holding-pool figure is in the headline and the leadership paragraph is in the second paragraph. The Cabinet Office has begun a leak inquiry. It will find nothing.

choices.label: Say nothing
choices.summary: The story runs its course; political cost.

choices.label: Publish the whole series
choices.summary: Candour is expensive, but willingness to serve edges up for a time.

title: The recruiting offices are busy
text: Regular recruiting has picked up sharply since the address. Applications are running well ahead of last year's intake of 7,771, and the recruiting partner is asking for staff. The applicants are volunteers. They are also untrained, and the pipeline that would train them is already full.

choices.label: Fast-track them
choices.summary: Costs money for extra assessment capacity; the regular pipeline gains a few hundred more entrants.

choices.label: Let the system cope
choices.summary: A smaller number get through the process this month.

source.name: MoD Service Personnel Statistics, 1 July 2026, Table 5a (Army untrained intake, 12 months to 30 June 2026)

title: Notices to quit
text: Before the crisis the Army was losing 3,311 trained soldiers a year to voluntary outflow. The regimental sergeant-majors report that applications to leave rose sharply this month, mostly from experienced corporals and sergeants who can see what is coming. Nobody is obliged to stay.

choices.label: Offer a retention payment
choices.summary: Costs money; a few hundred withdraw their notice.

choices.label: Let them go
choices.summary: The field army loses a few hundred experienced soldiers, and some junior leaders with them.

source.name: MoD Service Personnel Statistics, 1 July 2026, Tables 4 and 5d (Army trade-trained voluntary outflow, 12 months to 30 June 2026)

title: An Opposition day
text: The Opposition has tabled a motion of no confidence in the mobilisation programme rather than in the Government, so a backbencher can vote for it without bringing anything down. Those who voted for the Bill are asking what it would cost them to abstain. The Chief Whip asks what you can offer them.

choices.label: Whip it hard
choices.summary: Probably survives, with a little credit; if it does not, the cost is heavy.

choices.label: Concede an independent review
choices.summary: A small cost now and a review that will report after the deadline.

title: The trace reports
text: The tracing exercise is producing results. Letters have gone to every address held; a proportion have come back marked gone away, a proportion have been answered, and a small number have been answered by widows. Of the 60,245 people with a liability but no current record, the Department will never find most. It has found some.

source.name: Derived: 95,000 Strategic Reserve liability (Forces News, 15 January 2026) less 34,755 tracked (MoD SPS 1 July 2026, Table 8a)

title: Junior entry, considered
text: The Army has circulated a proposal to expand junior entry at the Foundation College. The note observes that non-completion there averaged 34% over the last published period, the worst of any training establishment. It also observes that a recruit taken at sixteen cannot be deployed until eighteen. That is a lead time of 24 months, against a deadline shorter than that. The proposal has been filed.

source.name: Forces News, 13 November 2025 (AFC Harrogate non-completion 2018–2023); minimum deployment age of 18

title: The women clause
text: The Bill excludes women. The Department's polling file records that 72% of the public supported including them when last asked. The population tables show that excluding them roughly halves the eligible pool. The Opposition has noticed both figures. An amendment is available to you.

source.name: YouGov daily results, 26 January 2024; ONS mid-2025 population estimates for England and Wales (MYE2)

title: The peacetime standard
text: In the nineteen months to last January the Army rejected 45,680 applications on medical grounds. The call-up is applying the same standard to the cohort and getting the same answer. The Surgeon General notes that a standard designed to keep people out of a volunteer army was never designed to let them into a conscript one.

choices.label: Relax the standard
choices.summary: The eligible pool grows, training attrition rises a little, and the usual political cost applies.

choices.label: Keep it
choices.summary: Nothing changes.

source.name: Written question 116544 (James Cartlidge MP), answered 9 March 2026: Army applications rejected on medical grounds, 5 July 2024 to 31 January 2026

title: The queue at vetting
text: United Kingdom Security Vetting is taking applications at several times the rate it was built for, and the queue is now counted in months rather than weeks. Nobody enters training without a clearance, so the queue is the call-up. The Home Office observes that the same teams clear police officers, prison officers and the agencies, and that the backlog is not yours alone.

choices.label: Give the military priority
choices.summary: Service applicants go to the front of the queue and clearances keep pace with the call-up; the Home Office will have something to say about the rest of the queue.

choices.label: Lower the threshold
choices.summary: A shorter check, applied faster: the call-up is not held back, and a backlog of cleared volunteers is released into the regular pipeline.

choices.label: Leave it to them
choices.summary: The queue clears at its own pace over the next half-year, and until it does the monthly call-up cannot run ahead of what vetting can clear.

title: The Commissioner writes
text: The Commissioner has written to the Home Secretary and copied the letter to you. Police recruitment has stalled: officers who passed their boards in the spring are still waiting on clearances that now go to the Army first, and two forces have started to lose candidates to other work. The letter is polite, detailed, and already with the Lobby.

choices.label: Return the police their slots
choices.summary: Vetting goes back to a shared queue; the call-up is held to what the teams can clear for the next half-year, and the Home Secretary is satisfied.

choices.label: Hold the priority
choices.summary: The Army keeps the queue. The letter is published, the Home Office briefs against the Department, and the police numbers will be remembered if the division is not raised.

title: The one who got through
text: A recruit cleared under the shortened check has been arrested at his depot. He had been dismissed from a police force for cause, and had written things in public that the old check would have found in an afternoon. The Ministry of Defence Police want to know how many more like him are in training, and so does everybody else.

choices.label: Re-screen the whole intake
choices.summary: The full check is restored and everyone cleared since the change is screened again; the call-up is held down while it is done, and it is not cheap.

choices.label: Say it was one man
choices.summary: The shortened check stays. The story runs for weeks, the Department is asked each day how many more there are, and willingness to serve falls with it.
